Motivation / Background

Fixes #58838.

where(attr: nil) always emitted IS NULL, even when normalizes ..., apply_to_nil: true turns nil into a non-nil value such as "". On a NOT NULL column that query matches nothing, and where.not(attr: nil) matches every row.

Detail

If the attribute type has a normalizer, QueryAttribute#nil? now uses the normalized database value. nil that normalizes to "" queries as name = '', same as where(attr: ""). A normalizer that maps blank to nil still queries with IS NULL.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Prepared statements promise a significant performance gain.

This Pull Request has been created because many statements are marked as unpreparable in Rails: many methods in Arel or elsewhere use SqlLiteral under the hood, which automatically mark the Arel collector as not preparable. This should be configurable.

Detail

This Pull Request changes Arel::Nodes::SqlLiteral so it can opt-in to being preparable. The resulting changes in the ToSql Visitor are implemented and aliases built by AliasPredication#as as now considered as preparable.

items.content_html:
Followup #51951

cc @jeremy @tenderlove @tomrossi7

Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because process: cannot vary per record, while the preprocessed: option it replaces could.

#51951 introduced process: with three static modes and deprecated preprocessed: for removal in Rails 9.0. But preprocessed: accepts a Symbol or a Proc called with the record:

attachable.variant :thumb, resize_to_limit: [4, 4], preprocessed: :should_preprocess?

There is no equivalent under process:, so an application that decides per record has
no migration path and has to keep calling the deprecated option — and will lose the behaviour entirely in 9.0.

My use case is the following : I have a Document model that has_one_attached :file with variants. and belongs to polymorphically to an attachable, and I have a strategy / variant per "attachable, for some I want them lazy while others need the later strategy.

Detail

This Pull Request changes ActiveStorage::NamedVariant#process so that, along with :immediately, :later, and :lazily, the :process option also accepts a Proc or the name of a method on the record. Either one is called with the record and returns one of the three modes:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_one_attached :avatar do |attachable|
    attachable.variant :thumb, resize_to_limit: [100, 100],
      process: ->(user) { user.public_profile? ? :later : :lazily }

    attachable.variant :medium, resize_to_limit: [300, 300],
      process: :medium_process_mode
  end

  def medium_process_mode
    public_profile? ? :later : :lazily
  end
end

Additional information

A value that doesn't resolve to a mode now raises ArgumentError, with the same wording as the existing :analyze option. Previously an unknown symbol was returned as-is and silently behaved like "never process

items.content_html:
Stacked on #58828, which drops the explicit SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS statements from the load. This PR is based on that branch, so its diff shows only the last commit. Supersedes #58681.

Motivation / Background

db:schema:load with config.active_record.schema_format = :sql on MySQL runs:

mysql --execute "SOURCE db/structure.sql" --database app_development

MySQL 9.4.0 added the --commands option to the mysql client. It is off by default in the 9.x and 26.x series, including the 9.7 LTS, and disables the client's local commands, including source, so the command above fails with:

ERROR 1064 (42000) at line 1: You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 'SOURCE db/structure.sql' at line 1

The 8.0.43+ and 8.4.6+ clients also have the option but default it to on, and MariaDB clients do not have it, so only Oracle clients from 9.4 on are affected. Homebrew's mysql and mysql-client formulas follow the 9.x and 26.x series, so brew install mysql on macOS installs an affected client. Distribution packages are still on 8.0 or 8.4 (Ubuntu 26.04 ships 8.4, RHEL 10 ships 8.4), but Ubuntu 26.10 has 9.7 in proposed, so this reaches Linux over time.

Detail

MySQLDatabaseTasks#structure_load now passes the structure file to the client's standard input, as SQLiteDatabaseTasks#structure_load already does:

mysql --database app_development < db/structure.sql

Reading SQL from standard input needs no client-side command, so the --commands setting does not matter, and structure_load_flags are passed through unchanged. Measured with rails new applications using schema_format = :sql, db:schema:load before and after this change:

mysql client --commands before after
Oracle MySQL 8.4.10 present, on by default OK OK
Oracle MySQL 26.7.0 present, off by default ERROR 1064 OK
MariaDB 12.3 not present OK OK

Why not --commands. Adding --commands to the command line only works with Oracle clients that have the option. MariaDB clients reject it. Measured with the MariaDB 12.3.2 client on Debian 13, where mysql is the MariaDB binary:

$ mysql --commands --execute "SELECT 1"
mysql: Deprecated program name. It will be removed in a future release, use '/usr/bin/mariadb' instead
mysql: unknown option '--commands'
$ echo $?
2

Rails cannot tell which vendor the mysql on PATH belongs to, so --commands cannot be the default.

A new test in the mysql2 and trilogy rake tests runs a real load through standard input against the test database and asserts the table exists. The other tests keep mocking Kernel.system and only had their expected command line updated.

Additional information

Workaround on released Rails versions. Applications that hit this with an Oracle mysql client 9.4 or later can add --commands to the structure load flags, for example in an initializer:

ActiveRecord::Tasks::DatabaseTasks.structure_load_flags = ["--commands"]

Applications with more than one adapter can use the hash form keyed by adapter name, for example { mysql2: ["--commands"] }. This works with Oracle clients 8.0.43+, 8.4.6+, 9.4+ and 26.x only, since MariaDB clients reject the option as shown above.

ecto_sql made the same move from SOURCE inside --execute to standard input (elixir-ecto/ecto_sql#684, elixir-ecto/ecto_sql#706).

References:

  • MySQL 9.4.0 release notes, "Added the mysql client --commands option ... This option is disabled by default." (WL #16949): https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/mysql/9.4/en/news-9-4-0.html
  • MySQL 8.0.43 and 8.4.6 release notes (2025-07-22), same option, "enabled by default": https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/mysql/8.0/en/news-8-0-43.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/mysql/8.4/en/news-8-4-6.html
  • mysql client options reference for --commands, default FALSE, lists source among the disabled commands: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/9.4/en/mysql-command-options.html#option_mysql_commands
  • mysql/mysql-server@0471004 "WL#16949: A mysql command line option to disable all built-in commands" and its 8.0 backport mysql/mysql-server@04c191b
  • client/mysql.cc defaults per branch: opt_commands = true on 8.0 and 8.4, false on 9.7 (LTS) and trunk

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

MySQLDatabaseTasks#structure_load runs SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0 before loading the structure file:

mysql --execute "SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0; SOURCE db/structure.sql; SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 1" --database app_development

The statement dates from the first Rails commit, db045db, whose clone_structure_to_test task read a structure file that Rails had written itself from SHOW CREATE TABLE output and ran it one statement at a time. Tables came in SHOW TABLES order, so a CREATE TABLE could reference a table that did not exist yet, and Rails had to turn the checks off itself.

ccc6910 switched the dump to mysqldump in 2012. Every dump written by mysqldump since MySQL 4.1.1 (mysql/mysql-server@f32299279d9, 2003) starts with

/*!40014 SET @OLD_FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=@@FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS, FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=0 */;

and ends with /*!40014 SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=@OLD_FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS */;. That commit predates the MariaDB fork and is in MariaDB/server under the same hash, so mariadb-dump has always written it too. --skip-comments, which structure_dump passes, only drops the informational -- comments, not these. So the load already runs with foreign key checks off, and the statement Rails adds has been redundant since 2012.

Detail

structure_load no longer sends the SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS statements, so the command becomes mysql --execute "SOURCE db/structure.sql" --database app_development. The checks are off while the file runs and the setting ends with the session, as before. Nothing touches the global value in either case.

Since the load now relies on the dump tool for the toggle, a new test in the mysql2 and trilogy rake tests runs a real structure_dump against the test database and asserts that both the header and the footer are in the file. On CI this exercises mariadb-dump, which is what default-mysql-client installs on Debian; locally it exercises whichever mysqldump is on PATH. The other rake tests keep mocking Kernel.system and only had their expected command line updated.

--compact in structure_dump_flags makes mysqldump leave the header and footer out (measured with mysqldump 26.7.0; --skip-opt, --skip-set-charset, --set-gtid-purged=OFF, --no-tablespaces and --column-statistics=0 keep them). Such setups can add the statement back on load, as the CHANGELOG entry says:

ActiveRecord::Tasks::DatabaseTasks.structure_load_flags = ["--init-command=SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0"]

Additional information

client/mysqldump.c per release: absent in every 4.0.x tag and in 4.1.0, present from 4.1.1 (2003-12-01) on. In MariaDB it is present from the first tag, mariadb-5.1.38-beta, through main.

This came up while moving the load off SOURCE, which MySQL clients from 9.4 on reject by default. The obvious replacement, --init-command, would collide with any --init-command a user passes through structure_load_flags, because the client keeps only the last one. Rather than merging them, it turned out Rails does not need the statement at all. The SOURCE change is stacked on this PR.

Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.

items.content_html:
I am sharing this PR for early feedback on my approach. Do y'all think this is a good high-level architecture to pursue?

About the boot performance, as discussed in Hakodate, I'd be interested to look in what it would take to support precompiling templates with Bootsnap, making parsing performance less important. - @byroot https://x.com/_byroot/status/2052666788446412954 (May 8, 2026)

Problem

Rails compiles templates the first time they are rendered in each process, causing cold-render times to be higher, most evident when an application is regularly deployed/booted. Introducing Herb to Rails exacerbates this problem, as Herb template compilation is roughly an order of magnitude slower than Erubi:

Template Size Erubi Herb Added Ratio
Tiny 58 B 3.9 µs 28.3 µs +24 µs 7.2x
Small 250 B 10.4 µs 116.1 µs +106 µs 11.2x
Medium 1 KB 24.4 µs 365.6 µs +341 µs 15.0x
Large 3 KB 81.7 µs 1,059.7 µs +978 µs 13.0x

At GitHub, we use @jhawthorn's https://github.com/jhawthorn/actionview_precompiler to shift this work to boot time (I've opened a PR to upstream it into core: #57234). However, with the introduction of Herb, compiling our templates at boot time more than doubled, an unacceptable increase in our production environment.

Proposed solution

This PR introduces a build-time cache for erb template handler output (but could be expanded to all handlers). In testing, it brought Herb to be more or less in line with Erubi at boot time:

Handler Cache Time
Erubi Off 15.138s
Erubi On 13.118s
Herb Off 25.167s
Herb On 13.335s

Cache loading costs about 0.177s.

  • Erubi: cache improves median by 13.2%.
  • Herb: cache improves median by 47.9%.
  • With cache enabled, Herb adds only 1.5% to median time.
  • Without cache, Herb is 69.1% slower.

To be clear, this PR does not provide the same performance improvements as actionview_precompiler. It only serves to eliminate the added overhead of using a slower ERB handler such as Herb.

Alternatives considered

I looked at adding this functionality to bootsnap, but found that template compilation needs the Rails application to be booted which is something bootsnap does not currently do.

Future work

We could eventually incorporate pieces of actionview_precompiler into this caching step.
items.title: [DO NOT MERGE] Add cache for erb template handler output

items.content_html:
Preloading has_many :top_posts, -> { order(:score).limit(3) } batched every owner into one WHERE author_id IN (?, ?, ...) ORDER BY score LIMIT 3, so three posts came back in total and most owners ended up with an incomplete or empty target.

Run the scope once per owner in a LATERAL subquery instead, correlated on the association key, under the same
config.active_record.respect_association_scope_limits as eager_load. Gating only one of the two would leave includes choosing between a strategy that applies the limit and one that ignores it, which is the inconsistency these changes exist to remove.

Like eager_load, this asks the database for nothing but LATERAL (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0.14+).
items.title: Apply an association scope's `limit`/`offset` per record in `preload`

items.content_html:
Eager loading has_many :top_posts, -> { order(:score).limit(3) } built its join out of the scope's WHERE predicates alone, dropping the limit, the offset and the order that decides which rows the limit picks, so every author came back with all of their posts.

Run the scope once per owner in a LATERAL subquery instead, where its limit and offset apply to that owner's own records.

Not every database has LATERAL: among the adapters Rails ships, PostgreSQL and MySQL 8.0.14+. Rather than changing what these associations return for everyone and giving half of them a different answer than the other half, put it behind config.active_record.respect_association_scope_limits, disabled by default. Third-party adapters can take part: Oracle has LATERAL too, and a database that writes the same thing as CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY, such as SQL Server, only needs its visitor to render it that way.
items.title: Apply an association scope's `limit`/`offset` per record in `eager_load`

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Four Arel node classes carry state that changes the SQL they emit, but inherit eql?/hash from Arel::Nodes::Binary/Unary, which compare only the class and operands:

Node Ignored state SQL it controls
Matches, DoesNotMatch escape, case_sensitive ESCAPE clause; LIKE vs ILIKE (PostgreSQL)
Regexp, NotRegexp case_sensitive ~ vs ~* (PostgreSQL)
InfixOperation operator any infix operator: >, <, ->>, @> …
UnaryOperation operator any prefix operator

Two such nodes are both eql? and hash-equal while rendering different SQL. ActiveRecord::Relation::WhereClause deduplicates predicates with Array#- and Array#|, so one of them is discarded. Relation#or is the worst case: self - other comes back empty, the idempotency shortcut fires, and the Or node is never built. The receiver is returned unchanged.

title = Post.arel_table[:title]
a = Post.where(title.matches("100%", "!"))
b = Post.where(title.matches("100%"))

a.or(b).to_sql
# before: SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts" WHERE "posts"."title" LIKE '100%' ESCAPE '!'
# after:  SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts" WHERE ("posts"."title" LIKE '100%' ESCAPE '!' OR "posts"."title" LIKE '100%')

a.merge(b).to_sql
# before: ... WHERE "posts"."title" LIKE '100%' ESCAPE '!'
# after:  ... WHERE "posts"."title" LIKE '100%' ESCAPE '!' AND "posts"."title" LIKE '100%'

The same collapse happens for InfixOperation.new(:">", …) against InfixOperation.new(:"<", …), and on PostgreSQL merges a case-sensitive LIKE with a case-insensitive ILIKE. There is no exception or warning; the resulting SQL is valid but narrower than requested.

This is reachable through the documented Arel::Predications#matches, #matches_regexp and Arel::Nodes::InfixOperation APIs. Rails' own query builders never construct these nodes with differing extra state, so no query generated by Active Record itself changes.

Detail

Each of the four classes gets an eql?/hash that folds in its own state, following the idiom already used by Extract, NamedFunction and NamedWindow:

def hash
  super ^ [@escape, @case_sensitive].hash
end

def eql?(other)
  super &&
    self.escape == other.escape &&
    self.case_sensitive == other.case_sensitive
end
alias :== :eql?

The re-alias is required because Binary's alias :== :eql? binds == to the parent implementation. super in eql? keeps the self.class == other.class check, so DoesNotMatch still differs from Matches, NotRegexp from Regexp, and Addition from a raw InfixOperation.new(:+, …).

38 lines across the four node files, no visitor or public API changes.

Tests: a new matches_test.rb covering Matches and Regexp inequality on each field plus a same-ivars control; a differing-operator case added to infix_operation_test.rb and unary_operation_test.rb (the existing inequality tests there only varied the operand); and a Relation#or regression test in or_test.rb for the user-visible symptom. All six new tests fail without the lib change.

Additional information

Present since Arel was merged into Active Record in 17ca170, so every release from 6.0.0. matches.rb is logically unchanged since that commit.

Run locally with ARCONN=sqlite3: full test/cases/arel/** (801 runs, 0 failures), the or/merging/where_clause/where/relations suites (0 failures), and rake test:sqlite3 (0 failures). MySQL and PostgreSQL rely on CI; the change is adapter-independent since only node equality is touched.

Rejected alternative: reflecting over instance_variables in Binary#hash/#eql? would fix this class of bug permanently, but hash/eql? on Arel nodes are on the hot path for every where/merge, and it would silently change equality for nodes that deliberately exclude fields (Arel::Table#hash excludes aliases).

items.content_html:
where.associated matches the association with a join, so for a collection association the result set is multiplied by the number of associated records:

Post.where.associated(:comments).pluck(:id)
# => [1, 1, 1, 2]

where.missing, its counterpart, returns each record only once, and returning duplicated records was already treated as a bug for ids in #46503.

Adding DISTINCT would fix the duplicates, but it leaks into the rest of the query as well (pluck, or order on a joined column), so collection associations are now matched with a correlated EXISTS subquery instead:

SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts"
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "comments" WHERE "comments"."post_id" = "posts"."id")
items.title: Fix `where.associated` to not return duplicated records

items.content_html:
where.missing left outer joins the association and matches the rows the associated primary key is NULL for. That tells whether a given row has a match, not whether the record has one at all, and the two only agree while the association is reached with a single join: a record that has a match then has no NULL row left.

Reaching the association through another table breaks that, since the outer join then applies per row of that table. An author whose posts have comments, but who also has a post without any, is matched as missing comments:

SELECT "authors".* FROM "authors"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "posts" ON "posts"."author_id" = "authors"."id"
LEFT OUTER JOIN "comments" ON "comments"."post_id" = "posts"."id"
WHERE "comments"."id" IS NULL
authors.name posts.title comments.id
david p1 1
david p2 NULL

The second row matches, even though david does have comments. An association whose scope joins another table is matched wrong the other way around, since the inner join that scope adds drops the NULL rows the match relies on.

Those are now matched with a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery, which asks the question per record rather than per row:

SELECT "authors".* FROM "authors"
WHERE NOT (EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM "posts" INNER JOIN "comments" ON "comments"."post_id" = "posts"."id"
  WHERE "posts"."author_id" = "authors"."id"
))
items.title: Fix `where.missing` to match associations reached through another table with an anti join

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This fixes #44946: a has_one_attached/has_many_attached association declared with strict_loading: true raises ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError just from attaching a file to a new record, not from any actual application-level lazy loading.

Repro from the issue, still reproducible against current main:

class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one_attached :avatar, strict_loading: true
end

user = User.new(name: "Jason", avatar: blob)
user.save!
# => ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError: `User` is marked for strict_loading.
#    The ActiveStorage::Blob association named `:avatar_blob` cannot be lazily loaded.

The has_many_attached equivalent raises the same error, as does calling user.avatar.attach(blob) on a new record.

Root cause

has_one_attached generates a real has_one association (avatar_attachment) and a has_one through: association (avatar_blob) behind the avatar accessor. Active Storage defers actually finding/building and saving the attachment to an after_save { attachment_changes["avatar"]&.save } callback (ActiveStorage::Attached::Model), by which point the owner is no longer a new record.

That matters because Association#find_target? short-circuits (skipping any query, and so any strict-loading check) while the owner is still a new record with no foreign key to look up by. Active Storage's own has_many_attached path (CreateMany) builds its attachments eagerly, while the owner is still new, so it never hits this. has_one_attached's CreateOne, though, only resolves its attachment lazily from that after_save callback, so by the time CreateOne#find_attachment reads avatar_blob/avatar_attachment, and CreateOne#save writes them, the owner is already persisted and the short-circuit no longer applies. Both the read and the write reach violates_strict_loading?, and both raise, even though this is Active Storage's own internal bookkeeping, not the lazy loading strict_loading exists to catch.

has_many_attached's actual persistence (record.avatar_attachments = ...) also can't hit this, for an unrelated reason: CollectionAssociation#replace already wraps its own internal load_target call in skip_strict_loading before diffing the old/new arrays. HasOneAssociation#replace has no equivalent - it calls load_target directly - so the same class of internal read that's already tolerated on the collection side isn't tolerated on the singular side.

The fix

Association#skip_strict_loading already exists for exactly this kind of internal, non-app-facing association access (it's what CollectionAssociation#replace uses above); it was private, so Active Storage couldn't call it across the class boundary. I made it public and wrapped the internal reads/writes in ActiveStorage::Attached::Changes::CreateOne#find_attachment and #save with it, scoped to just the two associations Active Storage itself manages (avatar_blob/avatar_attachment). CreateOneOfMany (the has_many_attached per-blob subchange) needed no change - it isn't affected by this bug for the reasons above.

Test coverage

I added four tests to activestorage/test/models/strict_loading_test.rb: both attachment styles (constructor assignment, attach) for both has_one_attached and has_many_attached, confirming none of them raise and the attachment actually persists. I ran the existing two tests in that file to confirm real lazy-loading (as_json(include: ...) on a loaded record) still correctly raises.

Full Active Storage suite (sqlite3, Disk service):

351 runs, 1170 assertions, 0 failures, 17 errors, 0 skips

The 17 errors are all ActiveStorage::UnpreviewableError: No previewer found for blob ... content_type=video/mp4 in preview_test.rb/representation_test.rb. I confirmed these are pre-existing and unrelated by running the same three tests against an unmodified main (identical failures; a local MP4-previewer tooling gap, not this change).

Full Active Record associations suite, sqlite3_mem (since this touches shared Association code):

1605 runs, 5576 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips

Additional information

I considered fixing this one level deeper instead: wrapping HasOneAssociation#replace's own load_target call in skip_strict_loading, to match what CollectionAssociation#replace already does. That would generalize the fix beyond Active Storage to any has_one reassigned after its owner is no longer a new record.

I backed off that approach for this PR. HasOneThroughAssociation#replace completely overrides the base method and never calls load_target through it, so a real fix would need to touch two separate relations (has_one and has_one through:) with different internal logic, not one shared code path. That's a bigger, less-tested surface than the two Active Storage call sites this PR touches, and changes behavior for every has_one in every app rather than just Active Storage's own bookkeeping, which seemed too big and too risky to me.

items.content_html:
Before this change, max_age doesn't work as advertised: Since in_use connections are ignored by sequential_maintenance in the reaper, under high load, it can take a lot of reaper cycles to get all old connections disconnected, with no bounded time guarantee.

If we want uphold some sort of guarantee that connections will get recycled eventually, max_age has to be checked when a threads holds exclusive access to the connection.

AFAIK there's basically three ways this could be done:

  1. when the connection is acquired, either:
  • attempt to get a single connection, if it's expired, disconnect, reconnect
  • attempt to find a connection that's not expired, disconnecting expired ones
  1. when the connection is released: disconnect, leave the task of connecting again to either the reaper or the next acquirer
  2. a new async step in the connection's lifecycle, between release and acquire, which would make the retirement check. this sounds overkill

I went with making the check and disconnect on release / checkin, both to match the documentation and because I think that's the most sensible option.
items.title: Fix max_age under high load

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58778.

build_read_query_regexp anchored at the start of the string only:

/\A(?:[(\s]|#{COMMENT_REGEX})*#{Regexp.union(*parts)}/

So write_query? classified any SQL whose first keyword was a read keyword as a read, however many statements followed it:

write_query?=false  "SELECT 1; DROP TABLE users; --"
write_query?=false  "SELECT 1; UPDATE users SET admin = true"
write_query?=false  "SHOW TABLES; DELETE FROM users"
write_query?=false  "WITH t AS (SELECT 1) SELECT * FROM t; INSERT INTO x VALUES (1)"
write_query?=true   "DROP TABLE users"

Under while_preventing_writes none of those were refused. On PostgreSQL, whose simple query protocol runs every ;-separated statement, execute then ran the stacked statement. Verified against PostgreSQL 17 with a throwaway table:

before fix   write_query?(payload) = false
             execute under while_preventing_writes: NO ERROR RAISED
             table exists after: false

after fix    write_query?(payload) = true
             execute under while_preventing_writes: ReadOnlyError raised
             table exists after: true

Detail

The regexp now matches the whole string. A read query may still end in a semicolon, optionally followed by whitespace or comments, so the existing trailing-semicolon behaviour is unchanged. A semicolon anywhere else makes the SQL a write.

Changing build_read_query_regexp covers the MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite3 adapters together, since all three derive READ_QUERY from it and test it with !READ_QUERY.match?(sql).

Additional information

On severity. I do not think this is a security boundary, and I would rather say so than oversell it. Reaching it needs attacker-controlled SQL in execute with no binds, which is already arbitrary SQL execution. QueryIntent#write_query? describes itself as a heuristic that "examines the outermost SQL operation", and Arel-built selects short-circuit to false before the regexp is consulted, so only raw SQL strings get here. I read this as making the heuristic fail towards refusing rather than permitting. Happy to route it differently if you disagree.

The tradeoff. A semicolon inside a string literal now also counts, so SELECT * FROM t WHERE note = 'a;b' written as raw SQL is no longer allowed on a replica. This is called out in the CHANGELOG. The alternative is to skip quoted regions before looking for ;, which means tracking single quotes, double quotes, backslash escapes and PostgreSQL dollar-quoting in a method meant to be a cheap heuristic. I raised both options on the issue and went with the simpler one; glad to switch if you would prefer the precise version.

Cost, measured. The regexp scans the whole string rather than stopping after the leading keyword, which is about 0.2 microseconds more per call on a typical read query (29ms to 68ms per 200k matches). No catastrophic backtracking: a pathological 50KB query matches in under a millisecond, and unterminated-comment and many-semicolon inputs are both fast.

If the extra scan is unwelcome, a sql.include?(";") fast path in front of it keeps the current cost for semicolon-free SQL, at the price of moving the logic out of the shared regexp and into the three adapters.

Tests. Stacked writes after each read form, including comment-prefixed and CTE variants, plus a test pinning the trailing-semicolon cases that must keep working.

Run locally:

  • Full Active Record suite on sqlite3: 9839 runs, 35058 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 39 skips
  • adapter_prevent_writes, base_prevent_writes, query_intent, query_cache, database_selector, sanitize, and the sqlite3 and postgresql adapter prevent-writes cases: green on both sqlite3 and postgresql
  • RuboCop clean

  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #48375.

ActionDispatch::ServerTiming subscribes to Active Support notifications and writes a Server-Timing header. For each event name it currently does:

events_collection.sum(&:duration)

ActiveSupport::Notifications::Event#duration is inclusive: a parent event’s duration already contains the time spent in nested child events.

That is fine for a single event, but wrong when many events share a name and nest. Nested partials all publish render_partial.action_view. If _a renders _b:

Event Inclusive duration
_b 20ms
_a 40ms (includes _b)
sum 60ms for ~40ms wall clock

Chrome then shows render_partial.action_view larger than the request itself, which matches the report in #48375.

Why exclusive time (this PR)

For each event name we report the sum of exclusive durations:

exclusive(e) = duration(e) − sum(duration of direct same-name children)

For the example above:

exclusive(_a) = 40 − 20 = 20
exclusive(_b) = 20
total         = 40   # matches wall clock for that tree

This keeps the metric useful: “how much time did work under this notification name account for?” without counting the same wall-clock interval twice.

Why not drop render_partial.action_view?

That was suggested on the issue as a simpler way to stop the confusion. It would remove a misleading number, but also remove the signal people use to spot expensive nested partials (the original motivation for looking at Server-Timing here). Exclusive aggregation keeps the metric and makes it accurate.

Why not exclusive across all event names?

A partial often nests sql.active_record, cache_*, etc. If we subtracted every nested name from the parent, render_partial.action_view would exclude SQL time spent while rendering the partial. That is a bigger semantic change: each Server-Timing row would mean “self time only,” and rows would no longer answer “how long did this instrumentation span?”

This PR only adjusts nesting within the same event name. Cross-name nesting is unchanged:

  • A partial that runs SQL still includes that SQL in the partial duration
  • sql.active_record is still reported as its own row
  • Sibling partials still add up

That matches how Server-Timing rows are already understood today, while fixing the double-count that made one row exceed the request.

Before / After

Nested render_partial.action_view (outer sleep 20ms + inner sleep 20ms ≈ 40ms wall clock):

# Before: ~75ms  (~1.9× wall clock)  — inclusive sum
# After:  ~45ms  (~1.1× wall clock)  — exclusive sum (remainder is sleep overhead)

Flat (non-nested) sibling partials are unchanged: both approaches sum to ~wall clock.

Implementation notes

  • Events for one name are sorted by start time (parents before children when starts match)
  • A stack finds direct same-name children via start/end containment
  • Only direct children’s inclusive durations are subtracted (multi-level nests telescope correctly: A→B→C → total exclusive = A’s inclusive span)

Test plan

  • cd actionpack && bin/test test/dispatch/server_timing_test.rb
  • Nested same-name events are not double-counted
  • Sibling same-name events still accumulate
  • Nested different-name events (e.g. SQL inside a partial) are not subtracted from the parent name
  • Standalone repro: ruby server_timing_nested_partials_48375_test.rb
items.title: Fix #48375: Server-Timing double-counting of nested same-name events

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This PR is a remake of the original #50039 by @monorkin. The motivation and the approach stay the same:

Currently, ActionCable doesn't have a mechanism to detect if its connection is half-open (if there is a client listening on the other end).
This PR changes the protocol so that a client has to respond to a PING message with a PONG message. If it doesn't do so within 2 heartbeats (6 sec) the connection is assumed to be half-open and is closed.

The original implementation was ported to the new Action Cable architecture with some changes and simplifications (see below).

Closes #50039
Fixes #45112

Detail

The new Ping-Pong flow in a nutshell:

  • Negotiation: The client connects to the server and specifies the additional sub-protocol, actioncable-ext-pong; if the server recognizes it, it adds the extensions: ["pong"] to the welcome message; thus, we guarantee compatibility between old clients and new servers and vice versa. This makes this feature an opt-in extension that could be combined with other potential future features (no version change required).

  • Heartbeats: If the client and the server agreed on pongs, they MUST: 1) the client sends back the ping message as command: "pong"; 2) the server checks if the client hasn't sent pings for 2*HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL, it's considered unresponsive and is disconnected with the no_pong reason.

Additional information

@monorkin
Changes compared to the original PR:

  • A feature protocol instead of a new protocol version (explain above)
  • The no_pong disconnect reason is used to match the AnyCable's one (AnyCable had this feature for a while, and I think, it makes sense to have parity here)
  • No instrumentation and latency tracking.

Re: instrumentation. I consider it out of scope (could be done later), since it doesn't solve the actual problem. Even more, implementing it in your app is just a couple of method—I specifically left an escape hatch for that:

class Connection < ApplicationCable::Connection
  def beat
    @pinged_at = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
     super
  end

  def handle_pong(_message)
    return unless @pinged_at
    latency = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - @pinged_at
    ActiveSupport::Notifications.instrument("pong.action_cable", latency:)
  end
end

@ioquatix
Some changes to the Socket interface. New methods expected:

  • Socket#extensions: Array — negotiated extensions (or [])
  • Socket#unresponsive?: bool — it's the server responsibility to detect responsiveness (since we need the actual time of messages arrival and control the ping loop)
  • Socket#close! — force-close (don't wait for closing acks); only called if unresponsive? returns true.

Neither if these is required for async-cable to work today (guarded by respond_to?).

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

upsert_all adds the relation's scope attributes to the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause, so rows that already exist get those columns rewritten even though the caller never passed them. On a model with default_scope { where(deleted_at: nil) } that restores every soft deleted row the upsert touches, without an error and without callbacks:

INSERT INTO "posts" ("id","title","deleted_at") VALUES (1, 'new', NULL)
ON CONFLICT ("id") DO UPDATE SET "title"=excluded."title","deleted_at"=excluded."deleted_at"

default_scope documents the opposite, "It is not applied while updating a record", and update_all on the same relation puts the scope in WHERE and never in SET. This is not a regression, the SQL is the same on 6.1.7.9, 7.0.8.5 and main.

Fixes #58796

Detail

updatable_columns is now built from the keys the caller passed, minus the scope keys. Scope columns are dropped from the update clause whether or not the payload carries them, so a minimal payload and one built from record.as_json both leave the existing row alone. The values list is untouched, so rows being inserted still get the full scope and author.books.insert_all keeps stamping author_id.

Measured on main (dd762fb) and on this branch:

main this PR
Post.upsert_all([{ id: 1, title: "new" }]) on a soft deleted row restored left alone
the same with deleted_at in the payload restored left alone
Scoped.insert_all([{ name: "x", format: "ebook" }]) "paperback" "paperback"
Scoped.insert_all([{ name: "x" }]) "paperback" "paperback"
author.books.insert_all([{ name: "x", author_id: other.id }]) author.id author.id
author.books.upsert_all over a row owned by someone else reassigned left alone

Additional information

Two things worth flagging:

  1. A scope column the caller passes is now ignored on the update branch rather than written, and update_only: or unscoped is the way to write it on purpose. Dropping only the keys the caller omitted would not be enough, a payload built from record.as_json carries deleted_at and would still resurrect the row.
  2. on_duplicate: :update degrades to :skip when the only updatable columns were scope columns, which changes affected row counts and returning. Happy to shape that differently if you would rather keep the statement a no-op UPDATE.

The related question, whether an attribute the caller passes should take precedence over the scope on the insert path, is deliberately left out. That is #44316, still open, where @skipkayhil asked for a deprecation cycle. Nothing here touches the insert path.
